title: British Library
description: National library of the United Kingdom
wiki_lead:
The British Library is the national library of the United Kingdom. Based in London, it is one of the largest libraries in the world, with an estimated collection of over 200 million items from multiple countries. As a legal deposit library, it receives copies of all books produced in the United Kingdom and Ireland, as well as a significant proportion of overseas titles distributed in the United Kingdom. The library operates as a non-departmental public body sponsored by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.
The British Library is a major research library, with items in many languages and in many formats, both print and digital: books, manuscripts, journals, newspapers, magazines, sound and music recordings, videos, play-scripts, patents, databases, maps, stamps, prints, drawings. The Library's collections include around 14 million books, along with substantial holdings of manuscripts and items dating as far back as 2000 BC. The library maintains a programme for content acquisition and adds some three million items each year occupying 9.6 kilometres (6 mi) of new shelf space.
The Library's purpose-built building stands next to St Pancras station in London. It was officially opened by Elizabeth II on 25 June 1998, and is classified as a Grade I listed building "of exceptional interest" for its architecture and history. Off-site storage is provided at a second site near Boston Spa in Yorkshire.

History


Early foundations  (1972–1997)
The British Library was created on 1 July 1973 after the passing of the British Library Act 1972. Before this, the national library was part of the British Museum, which provided the bulk of the holdings of the new library, alongside smaller organisations which were folded in (such as the National Central Library, the National Lending Library for Science and Technology and the British National Bibliography). In 1974 functions previously exercised by the Office for Scientific and Technical Information were taken over; in 1982 the India Office Library and Records and the HMSO Binderies became British Library responsibilities. In 1983, the Library absorbed the National Sound Archive, which holds many sound and video recordings, with over a million discs and thousands of tapes.
The core of the Library's historical collections is based on donations and acquisitions from the 18th century known as the "foundation collections", and include the books and manuscripts of Sir Hans Sloane (d. 1753), whose decision to donate his library and natural history collection to the nation led to the formation of the British Museum. The museum trustees purchased the Harleian Library collection of Robert Harley (d. 1721) for £10,000; Also provided to the library was the Cotton library, the former collection of Sir Robert Cotton (d. 1631); this was in public possession and had been housed at Ashburnham House, Westminster. These collections were added to by the Old Royal Library, donated by George II, and the King's Library of George III.

For many years its collections were dispersed in various buildings around central London including Bloomsbury (within the British Museum), Chancery Lane, Bayswater, and Holborn, with an interlibrary lending centre on Thorp Arch Trading Estate near Boston Spa, 2.5 miles (4 km) east of Wetherby in West Yorkshire, and the newspaper library at Colindale, north-west London.


Move to St Pancras (1997–present)
Initial plans for the British Library required demolition of an integral part of Bloomsbury – a 7-acre (2.8 ha) swathe of streets immediately in front of the Museum, so that the Library could be situated directly opposite. After a long and hard-fought campaign led by  George Wagner, this decision was overturned and the library was instead constructed by John Laing plc on a site at Euston Road next to St Pancras railway station.

grok_lead: The British Library is the national library of the United Kingdom, established by the British Library Act 1972 and commencing operations on 1 July 1973 as a result of the separation of the British Museum's library departments into an independent institution. It serves as the country's principal research library, preserving and providing access to a vast collection exceeding 170 million items, including printed books, manuscripts, journals, newspapers, maps, sound recordings, patents, stamps, and born-digital materials. As the central legal deposit library under UK law, it receives a compulsory copy of every publication produced in the United Kingdom and Ireland, ensuring a comprehensive national archive of published output regardless of format or language. The Library's origins trace back to the collections of the British Museum, founded in 1753, which included foundational holdings such as the King's Library of George III and the Cottonian collection, formed in the early 17th century by Sir Robert Bruce Cotton. Following its establishment, the British Library consolidated these resources with other specialized collections, including those from the British Museum, the Patent Office Library, and the National Central Library, to form one of the world's largest and most comprehensive repositories of knowledge. Its mission encompasses not only preservation but also research support, digital innovation, and public engagement, operating as a free public institution open to everyone for reference and study. The Library maintains two primary sites: its flagship building at St Pancras in London, a purpose-built architectural landmark opened to the public in 1998 and housing reading rooms, exhibition galleries, and treasures like the Magna Carta and the Lindisfarne Gospels, and a major document storage and processing center in Boston Spa, West Yorkshire. With approximately 14 million books and e-books (as of 2025), over 310,000 manuscript volumes, 60 million patents, and 60 million newspaper issues (as of 2023) among its holdings, the collection continues to grow daily through legal deposit, purchases, and donations. Notable for its role in cultural preservation, the Library also manages initiatives like the UK Web Archive, capturing online content under legal deposit provisions, and supports global scholarship through digitization projects that have made millions of items freely accessible online.
